demand_source.title: Browser (OpenClaw-managed): What you get
demand_source.anchor: Question answering over readable page text
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw documents a separate, agent-only browser whose supported uses include answering questions from a page's readable text.

edits.description: The research helper can also read public pages that need JavaScript, logged out, and pull the text out of long articles, of videos that have captions and of podcasts that publish a transcript. An in-house hook keeps the browser read-only in code (one profile, no typing, no form filling, no uploads, no page scripts); bot walls and logins stop it.
edits.example: Jordan texts: "What does the rec centre page say about spring swim lessons?" The page shows nothing without JavaScript, so research opens it in the logged-out browser and her own agent relays the dates with the link. Or Tony texts a link to a 40-minute video that has captions and asks for the main points.
edits.how: Two readers, on the research agent only. (1) The `browser` tool on the managed `openclaw` profile, with `headless: true` on that profile and `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`. Four switches come first: `browser.enabled` (off since M0), the browser tool on research's sandbox tool allow list (it is on the sandbox default deny list), the per-agent tool allow, and a place for the browser to live. First choice is the roadmap's sandbox browser container with the LAN blocked; its image has to be built from a source checkout because the npm install does not include the Dockerfile. The fallback is the host's managed profile through `sandbox.browser.allowHostControl` and an explicit host target, which the docs say to keep off for sandboxed agents unless you trust them. (2) A host stdio MCP that wraps `summarize --extract --json` and returns extracted text from articles, and from YouTube videos and podcasts that publish captions or a transcript, without calling a model; the wrapper pins `--firecrawl off`, holds no third-party keys, sets up no transcription fallback and checks the address itself. The firewall (formerly WEB-03): an in-house plugin with `api.on("before_tool_call", handler, { matcher: ["browser"] })`, default-deny and failing closed. It rejects any `profile`, `target` or `node` other than the one assigned to the agent (a missing profile is filled in or blocked, because an omitted profile means the default one) and rejects `systemProfile`, `into`, `domains` and `dashboard`. Of the tool's 24 actions it allows only a listed read-only subset (for example status, tabs, open, navigate, focus, close, snapshot, text, screenshot). `act` and `upload` are not on that list in this build, which blocks every act kind at once: `batch`, `evaluate`, `press`, `clickCoords`, `drag`, `wait`, `resize`, `type`, `fill`, `select` and `click`. If a page later proves unreadable without scrolling, `act` comes back only for kinds on an allowlist of its own (`scrollIntoView`, `hover`), each with an eval case. The hook reads the URL from `targetUrl` first and `url` second, looks inside a nested `request` object, and blocks any call whose top-level and nested kinds differ. Unknown agent, missing field, unknown action or kind, or a parse error returns a block; the runner itself blocks the call if the handler throws or times out. Research reads the open web, so there is no site allowlist here; navigation stays http and https under the private-network block in F019 (formerly WEB-01). Not built here: the exact-hostname allowlist and the ask-a-parent-before-typing approval branch, whose only consumer is the roadmap's M6 jobs agent.
caveats: Bot walls, logins, CAPTCHAs and two-factor prompts stop it. The bundled browser skill tells the agent to report them as manual steps, and the docs say sandboxed browser sessions are more likely to be flagged as bots.

The sandbox browser image cannot be built from the npm install; it needs a source checkout. The host alternative needs allowHostControl, which the docs say to keep off for sandboxed agents unless you trust them.

The hook sees tool parameters, not page meaning: a click carries a snapshot ref, not the button's label, so code cannot tell 'Next' from 'Submit'. That is why clicks are blocked outright in this read-only build.
A navigation check in a hook sees the URL the agent asked for, not where redirects or page scripts go next; the private-network block in F019 is the backstop.
With open and navigate allowed, a link straight to a file is saved into the managed downloads directory without the download action ever being called.

The parameter names come from the installed 2026.9.7 browser tool schema and can change with any update. Default-deny keeps a new action blocked until someone allows it, but the hook needs a contract test after every OpenClaw update.

summarize runs on the host, outside the SSRF policy that covers web_fetch and the browser, and has its own third-party extraction fallbacks; the wrapper must switch those off and check the address itself.
An independent evaluation on live websites found web agents much less competent than earlier benchmarks suggested, so expect misses on complex pages.

The extractor uses published captions and podcast transcripts first; its README says transcription is a fallback that has to be configured. The wrapper holds no keys and sets none up, so expect nothing back for a video without captions or a podcast without a published transcript; local transcription would be a later add-on.
edits.safety: The research agent holds no private data, no memory and no accounts, and this browser is a managed profile with none of the family's signed-in sessions, so an injected page has nothing to steal. What a real browser adds is a way to act, so the limits on profile, target and actions live in code and fail closed, page script evaluation is off in config, and the home network is out of reach (the egress guardrails in F019). The hook is in-house code on the security boundary: one parsing mistake is a bypass, so it gets its own injection eval cases before the browser is switched on. No profile on this browser ever holds a login, and CAPTCHAs are reported, never solved.

demand_source.title: Talk mode
demand_source.anchor: Native Talk is a continuous loop
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw documents Talk in its phone apps as a supported continuous speech conversation: it listens, sends the transcript to the agent and speaks the reply.

edits.name: Talk mode on Tony's iPhone (native speech loop first, realtime voice as a later option; operator only)
edits.description: Tony installs the OpenClaw iPhone app and holds a spoken back-and-forth with his own agent: the phone transcribes, the gateway answers as it would a text, and the reply is spoken. The app also adds a Listen action on any reply and a Siri phrase or Action Button shortcut that starts voice. It is Tony's phone only: the app is a full gateway client and a device node, and nothing verified today can hold a second adult's phone to her own agent. A later option, realtime voice, swaps this loop for a live call between the phone and an OpenAI voice model: faster and interruptible, but the raw audio goes to OpenAI, it needs its own key and budget, and it is one switch for every iPhone Talk session on the gateway.
edits.how: The App Store OpenClaw app on Tony's iPhone, the same install and pairing as the iPhone app entry (OCL-01), reaching the gateway over the tailnet (the app connects over LAN or tailnet; this gateway is Tailscale Serve only). Before pairing (limits folded in from VOX-03): the phone command ceiling is in place (device commands denied first; see the iPhone app entry OCL-01 and the gateway-wide node deny list MAC-04); `talk.agentId` is set explicitly and names a memory-less agent, because it is one value for the whole gateway and receives every Talk session that arrives without an agent-prefixed key; `tts.modelOverrides.allowProvider` stays off (its default) so a reply directive cannot move speech to a cloud provider; and the operator's inspect script gains a read-only listing of paired devices and their scopes. Tony generates the pairing code with `openclaw qr --limited` instead of the default admin handoff. `--voice-node` is not for this phone: it drops the write scope, so typed chat (`chat.send`) and the Listen action (`tts.speak`) stop working, and whether Talk still runs is untested. Native Talk is a loop: Apple Speech recognition on the phone, Gateway chat on the agent picked in the app (tony-main), then `talk.speak` playback. `talk.speak` reads the Talk block, not the `tts` block: set `talk.provider` plus `talk.providers.<id>` to a speech provider (the local engine from VOX-04 can be named there); with no Talk provider the gateway call fails and the docs mention an iPhone system-voice fallback. Other keys: `talk.speechLocale`, `talk.silenceTimeoutMs`, `talk.interruptOnSpeech`. Entry points: the inline Talk control, the `Start Live Voice` App Shortcut, the Siri phrase, or the Action Button. Later option, realtime voice (was VOX-02): a `talk.realtime` block with `provider` openai, a realtime model from the installed docs, `transport` webrtc and `brain` agent-consult, so every tool call still goes through gateway policy on the agent. The iPhone path is client-owned WebRTC and needs an OpenAI Platform API key under `talk.realtime.providers.openai`, supplied as a SecretRef and separate from the per-person chat keys. Once that block is set, OpenAI realtime configs run as WebRTC on the iPhone and only non-realtime configs use the native loop. The host asks for a fresh spoken yes before a high-impact action started by voice.
depends_on: the OpenClaw iPhone app paired on Tony's phone with device commands denied first (OCL-01, and the node deny list in MAC-04)
Tailscale on the phone
a Talk speech provider under `talk.provider` (the VOX-04 local engine), or accept the iPhone system-voice fallback
decision: is a write-scoped gateway credential on Tony's phone acceptable
a written device-revocation step for a lost phone
a second adult's phone only after gateway.roles is proven with the iOS app on a test device
for the realtime option only: an OpenAI Platform key dedicated to voice with its own spend cap, and a decision on Zero Data Retention for the organisation that owns that key
caveats: Audio can leave the house even in the native loop: the docs say Apple Speech recognition on iOS may use network services. The transcript then goes to OpenAI as text like any typed message.
iOS may suspend background audio, so voice is best-effort unless the app is in the foreground; the Siri shortcut does not bypass unlock or foreground restrictions.
Dictating an iMessage to Happy with the keyboard microphone or Siri already works today with no setup. Talk adds the continuous loop, barge-in and spoken replies, not a new capability.

Everything about the pairing applies here unchanged and is spelled out in the iPhone app entry (OCL-01): the app is a gateway client first, every pairing profile includes operator.read (session lists, chat history, logs and read-only browsing of every agent's workspace), `--limited` removes only operator.admin and leaves write, approvals and Talk secrets, the phone registers as a node, App Store builds use a vendor-hosted push relay, and a lost phone has to be revoked on the gateway. On a second adult's phone the other adult's agent memory would be readable.
`--voice-node` does not rescue the native loop: the chat turn is chat.send, which the docs class as write-scoped, and that profile holds only read and talk.

Talk playback uses the Talk speech provider, not the general tts block. The docs name elevenlabs (cloud), mlx and system for Talk, and the mlx helper ships with the Mac app, which is not installed here; expect the iPhone's own system voice.

`openclaw qr` only advertises a Tailscale URL when OpenClaw itself owns the Serve route (`gateway.tailscale.mode`). The config repo sets it to serve on a loopback bind, so this looks met; confirm on the live gateway. mDNS discovery is off there, so pairing is by QR or setup code.

A phone paired without operator.admin cannot open the app's Settings pages, where this device's Talk, Voice Wake, background-listening and speakerphone switches live. Plan on the inline Talk control in Chat and the Start Live Voice shortcut.
There is no speaker identification anywhere in the stack: whoever is near the microphone is the user.

Realtime option: raw audio, not just text, goes to OpenAI for the whole call (with WebRTC the media runs directly between the phone and the provider), under 30 days of abuse-monitoring retention unless the organisation has Zero Data Retention; the M1 store-off setting covers chat calls only. It is billed separately from chat (OpenAI's price page lists gpt-live-1 at $0.05 a minute), and each turn handed to the agent adds normal chat cost.

Realtime option: `talk.realtime` is one gateway-wide block, and the docs say OpenAI realtime configs run as WebRTC on iOS while only non-realtime configs use the native loop, so it replaces the native loop instead of sitting beside it. The installed docs list the iPhone GPT-Live path as implemented with device live verification still pending, and GPT-Live sessions end at a 30-minute limit.

Realtime option: the spoken yes gates the action, not the speaker, so anyone in earshot can say it, and a room with children talking would be streamed to a cloud model. Use it with the phone at the ear or headphones, or stay on the native loop, which is enough for most questions; realtime mainly buys lower latency and being able to interrupt.
unverified: Whether Talk still runs on an iPhone paired with a `--voice-node` code. What is certain from the installed scope table is that such a phone loses typed chat and the Listen action (chat.send and tts.speak need the write scope).

Which speech providers pass the Talk-mode check inside `talk.speak`, and whether a local engine set up under tts (VOX-04) can serve as the Talk provider on iOS. The installed code resolves `talk.provider` against the general speech-provider registry with fallback disabled.
Whether a Talk session can continue the same conversation as the person's iMessage thread, or only shares agent memory.
Whether the iOS app can connect its operator session at all once `gateway.roles` is configured.
Whether Tony and Jordan have separate tailnet logins, which a verified Tailscale identity per person would need.
Whether the M0 Tailscale Serve route is owned by OpenClaw (`gateway.tailscale.mode`), which `openclaw qr` requires before it will advertise a tailnet URL.
Whether in-app Talk still works while the phone's node surface is left unapproved.
Whether Talk starts from the inline control on a limited pairing without a first visit to the admin-only Talk settings page, and when exactly the iPhone falls back to its system voice.

Realtime option: whether an iPhone can stay on the native loop while `talk.realtime` is configured; whether this OpenAI organisation has Zero Data Retention; what the bounded session history handed to the voice model contains for an agent that holds personal memory; and whether Talk configuration read with operator.talk.secrets includes the realtime provider key.
edits.safety: Tony's phone only. That is acceptable because section 1b of the roadmap already makes Tony the control-plane owner who can read everything; pair with the limited profile, keep the node surface unapproved, and treat the phone as an admin-adjacent credential. A second adult's phone has no safe placement today: the docs describe operator scopes as a guardrail inside one trusted operator domain, not a boundary between people, and the named-roles feature that could limit her to her own agent rejects the device and bootstrap tokens that QR pairing issues. Voice input is the speaker's own words, so no untrusted-content leg is added to tony-main, and tool policy, hooks and the family-only recipient pin still apply to the agent's tool calls. A child must not use this Talk session: every agent is cloud-backed and Apple Speech on iOS may send audio to Apple. The realtime option adds a second cloud model that hears the room and is given a bounded slice of the session's history. `brain: agent-consult` keeps tools behind the same policy, hooks and approvals as text, and the spoken-confirmation gate is host-enforced and used once, but it does not identify who spoke. Realtime is never pointed at a kids agent.

demand_source.title: Model Context Protocol Server - Home Assistant
demand_source.supports: Home Assistant's own integration is built so that an AI agent can control the devices a household has exposed and see the current state of the home. Opened in this run.

edits.name: Home Assistant as the house hub over MCP: Hue, Sonos and the TV on one list, plus announcements on the Sonos speakers
edits.description: One Home Assistant endpoint through which a stateless home agent reads state and controls only the entities a parent has exposed, covering Hue, Sonos and the LG TV with one audited list instead of one plugin per brand. It also adds something the direct command-line route has no command for: a parent texts an announcement and the Sonos speakers say it over the music, which is turned down and then restored. It is an alternative to the direct Hue and Sonos plugins (F076), not an addition: pick one path. It needs a Home Assistant VM on the Mac mini, which the roadmap already plans for the kids' speaker (VOX-11). OpenClaw 2026.9.7 has no Home Assistant, HomeKit, Matter or MQTT integration of its own; the way in is Home Assistant's own MCP Server integration.
edits.example: Are any lights or the TV still on downstairs? Or: 'announce: the bus leaves in ten minutes', and the living room and family room speakers say it.
edits.how: Run Home Assistant OS in a VM on the Mac mini (the roadmap already plans this VM for the kids' speaker). Add the Hue, Sonos and LG webOS integrations, then the 'Model Context Protocol Server' integration; turn off 'Expose all LLM APIs' and expose only the wanted entities. In OpenClaw add mcp.servers.<name> with url http://<ha-host>:8123/api/mcp, transport 'streamable-http' written out (when it is omitted OpenClaw uses sse), and the Home Assistant long-lived token in headers.Authorization, supplied through a secret reference and not a config literal (auth 'oauth' with openclaw mcp login is the documented alternative). This Gateway uses tools.profile 'minimal', which hides MCP tools, so grant them only to the stateless 'home' agent from F076 by listing the <server>__<tool> names in that agent's alsoAllow and in its sandbox tool allow list (tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow); no other agent then sees the server. Write toolFilter.include after a live probe (openclaw mcp doctor <name> --probe), since it selects tools by name. The registry before_tool_call hook stays as the second, fail-closed gate and enforces quiet hours. Announcements (was VOX-07): Home Assistant's Sonos integration plays speech with its `announce` option as an overlay, lowering the music and restoring the volume afterwards; it needs TCP port 1443 on each speaker to be reachable from the Home Assistant host. Because the MCP server offers intents and exposed scripts only, a parent writes one Home Assistant script that wraps the announce call and exposes it, and picks a local speech engine in Home Assistant, since its text-to-speech page also lists cloud engines. The trigger is deterministic: a `before_dispatch` claim on a fixed prefix such as `announce:` from an adult's handle, so no agent that reads web results decides to speak to the house. The code that claims the text then starts the Home Assistant script itself, with no model turn, through Home Assistant's REST API (`/api/services/<domain>/<service>` with the same host-side bearer token); that call path is a design choice and was not tried. The first version offers a short list of fixed phrases; the parent's own words, verbatim, come later, and model-written text never. Text length, volume, quiet hours (G001), a speaker allowlist and a daily cap are enforced in code.

A HomeKit accessory can pair with only one controller, so the LG TV stays in Apple Home and joins Home Assistant through the webOS integration, not through HomeKit.
Running both the direct CLIs and Home Assistant doubles the paths to the same lamp; pick one.
With only Hue, two Sonos speakers and one TV today, the hub pays off mainly if the announcements or the kids' speaker (VOX-11) are also wanted.

Home Assistant's macOS page documents VirtualBox (UTM only as a fallback for people used to virtual machines) and points anyone not comfortable with virtual machines to a dedicated board; the VM is one more service to patch, back up and bring back after every reboot and FileVault unlock, and until it is up every home tool fails.

Home Assistant's MCP server offers its Assist intents plus any scripts exposed to Assist, not arbitrary actions; anything beyond on/off, brightness, volume and state reads (announcements, TV notices) needs a script a parent writes and exposes.

Because those tools are generic intents, toolFilter.include narrows verbs, not device classes; the exposure list in Home Assistant and a before_tool_call check on each call's target are the real limits.

The long-lived token is a ten-year credential for Home Assistant's APIs as one user; the exposed-entity limit applies to the MCP tools, not to the token, so it must stay host-side and be rotated by hand.
State text returned by Home Assistant (now-playing titles, device names) is third-party text read by an agent that can actuate; allowlists and caps in code have to bound the result.

Home Assistant's MCP options 'Expose all LLM APIs' and 'Require an administrator account' are both on by default: out of the box every LLM API is offered and the token must belong to an administrator. Tighten the first before OpenClaw connects; a token for a non-admin Home Assistant user works only after the second is turned off.
Home Assistant exposes new entities in the cover domain (garage doors and gates) to Assist by default, so the exposure list needs a review after each device is added.
Announcements reach only the two Sonos speakers, which the 9 Oct scan placed in the living room and the family room, so nothing is heard in the kitchen or bedrooms.
Home Assistant's Sonos page warns that older Sonos hardware or S1 firmware may not fully support announcements; the two speakers here are unchecked.
A talking house at the wrong moment is worse than no feature: quiet hours and a low daily cap matter more than voice quality.

Without Home Assistant there is no good announcement route: Sonos documents its audio-clip command under the cloud Control API, which would put a Sonos account token on the gateway, and the sonos command-line tool has no announce command (its play-uri sets the speaker to the new audio and documents no way to bring the music back).
edits.safety: The home agent keeps no memory, has no web tool and no outbound message tool, so it holds no private data and cannot send anything out; the only outside text it reads is device state. Only exposed entities are reachable through MCP; locks, garage, alarm, gate and cameras are never exposed in Home Assistant, and a fail-closed hook that inspects each call's target repeats that block on the OpenClaw side. The token is a wider credential than the MCP tools and is kept host-side only. An announcement is heard by everyone in the house, guests and children included, so it is an outbound channel in its own right: it is triggered only by a fixed prefix from an adult's handle that code claims before any model runs, it never speaks model-written or web-derived text, and it is never reachable from the research or mail agents.
